$$
\begin{aligned}r &=p+tv,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

However, there is also another way, which is to write the **equation of a line using the cross product**, as follows:

$$
(\mathbf{r}-  \mathbf{p} ) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
$$

For example, suppose that we have a line that passes through the point $P(4,1,-5)$ and has a direction vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle 1,0,-1 \rangle$ (see the picture below).

![](images/6c/6cd052e948a46524e08b1305a59019b052e71c7b9ce6e5376f49c4cbcc56a737.png)

The equation of the line can be written as follows:

$$
(\mathbf{r}-\langle 4,1,-5 \rangle) \times \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle = \mathbf{0}
$$

To understand why the formula works, notice that for any point $R,$ this point lies on the line if and only if the vector $\overrightarrow{PR}$ is parallel to $\mathbf{v}.$ Now, we know that the cross product of two parallel vectors is always $\mathbf{0}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\overrightarrow{PR} \parallel \mathbf{v} 
	\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad 
	\overrightarrow{PR} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r &=p+tv,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}

However, there is also another way, which is to write the **equation of a line using the cross product**, as follows:

$$
(\mathbf{r}-  \mathbf{p} ) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
$$

For example, suppose that we have a line that passes through the point $P(4,1,-5)$ and has a direction vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle 1,0,-1 \rangle$ (see the picture below).

$$

$$
